title: What anointing does (CCC 1520–1523)
hook: strength, peace, courage, union with Christ's suffering

segments.voice: Yesterday, indulgence, taken honestly: not forgiveness, but healing for what's left after forgiveness. Your line was never for sale. Did the broken window come back to mind? Day one thousand one hundred four.

A hospital room, late afternoon. The television is muted. A woman in the bed has been told the surgery is tomorrow morning. A priest comes in with a small metal case, the size of a lipstick. He prays, lays his hands on her head in silence, and then, with his thumb, traces oil on her forehead and on the palms of her hands. It takes a few minutes. Nothing about the surgery changes. So what just happened? Some people think this sacrament is only for the last hour of life. The Catechism tells a wider story, and today we look at what it says the anointing actually does.
screen: `A HOSPITAL ROOM.` → `OIL ON THE FOREHEAD AND HANDS.` → `WHAT JUST HAPPENED?`

segments.voice: The roots are in the letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Notice the scene. Not a dying man alone. A sick person who calls the community in. The Catechism names what the sacrament gives. First, a gift of the Holy Spirit: strength, peace and courage to face the difficulties of serious illness or the frailty of old age. Not a guarantee of a cure. The Catechism does say healing of the body can come, if God wills it, but the first gift is inward: the strength not to be swallowed by fear or discouragement. Second, union with Christ's own suffering. This is the deep one. Catholic teaching says the sick person, joined to Christ, can find that their suffering takes on a new meaning. It isn't wasted. Paul, writing to the Colossians, speaks of rejoicing in his sufferings and of filling up in his own flesh what is lacking in Christ's sufferings, for the sake of the Church. Third, a gift for the Church. The sick person, the Catechism says, isn't only on the receiving end: by joining their suffering to Christ's, they contribute to the good of the whole people of God, and the Church prays for them in return. Fourth, for those near the end, a preparation for the last journey, completing the anointings that marked the whole of a Christian life, from baptism on. So the oil on that woman's forehead didn't move the surgery. It was meant to change who walks into it.
screen: `IS ANY MAN SICK AMONG YOU?` · `STRENGTH, PEACE AND COURAGE.` · `UNITED TO CHRIST'S SUFFERING.` · `A GIFT FOR THE WHOLE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit or call someone sick. Settle first, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is ill, or frail, or waiting on a diagnosis. Picture where they are right now: a bed, a waiting room, a kitchen chair. Think of one plain thing you could say to them that isn't advice. Then, if you can, reach out today: a call, a short message, a knock on the door. If you pray, you can ask God to give them strength, peace and courage. If you don't, just hold them in mind until the bell. The bell holds the time.
What anointing does. Strength, peace and courage in illness, union with Christ's suffering, a gift for the whole Church, and for some, a preparation for the last journey. Today's word.
Your line: strength in sickness. Today, make that call or send that message to the person you thought of, and keep it short and warm. Day one thousand one hundred four.

howItsDone: Catholics who are seriously ill, facing major surgery, or weakened by old age can ask a priest for the anointing of the sick, which can take place at home, in a hospital, or during a parish Mass for the sick.

CCC 1520–1523 paraphrased (copyrighted translation): strength, peace, courage; union with the passion; ecclesial grace; preparation for the final journey. 'Bodily healing if God wills it' reflects CCC 1520.
Hook scene (oil on forehead and palms, silent laying on of hands) describes the current Latin rite; confirm. 'Some people think this sacrament is only for the last hour' is kept general.
Original: ἔλαιον is the noun for oil in James 5:14 (the verb is ἀλείψαντες); confirm.
